subsubtopic: LIMIT OF PROTECTION FOR INVESTORS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) announced that he would introduce draft legislation soon to increase guarantee deposit insurance coverage. Agitation to increase the 1967 limit began as early as 1975. Astra Trust went broke in 1980, and still the Government refused an increase and called for a
study. The report of that study was in the hands of the appropriate Minister for more than a year, yet the Government refused to act.
The 1967 dollar upon which the $20,000 limit was based is now worth only 40 cents. Per capita savings in Canada are greater than they are in the United States. Now, after three more trust companies are shown to suffer from financial instability, the Government is struck with creeping paralysis.

subsubtopic: NECESSITY FOR "BUY CANADIAN" PRINCIPLE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Canadian shipyards have demonstrated a production capability that makes our shipbuilding industry equal or superior to the world-wide standard, yet over 2,000 shipyard workers are unemployed in the Maritimes, and thousands more across Canada. Canadian shipyards can compete internationally and for domestic orders if the ground rules are the same for all competitors. Unfortunately they are not.
Some shipbuilding nations subsidize employment. Others use their national banking system or treasury to assist ship construction. Canadian shipyards cannot compete for foreign or domestic orders in the face of such massive national subsidization. In order to maintain viability and secure thousands of skilled jobs, Government protection and help are required.
Here is part of the problem-East Coast resource exploration has created a huge demand for marine drilling rigs and service vessels, yet only the Sedco 709, among the 20 or more drilling rigs, is Canadian-built. Even Petro-Canada charters foreign built oil rigs and service vessels. Canada must have a shipbuilding policy that establishes a "Buy Canadian" principle for energy exploration and the fishery, as well as northern and coastal marine activity, thereby excluding non-Canadian vessels.
The Government policy must also provide realistic financial assistance to off-set the support provided in competing nations. Unless a Government shipbuilding policy provides adequate protection and assistance, a viable job-generating industry will be destroyed. The proposed shipbuilding policy does not meet this test.

subsubtopic: DESIGNATION OF COMMUNITIES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is well known that certain Canadian communities are experiencing more economic pain than others as a result of the present recession/depression. In an effort to provide special support to those communities especially hard hit, the Government of Canada established the Industry and Labour Adjustment Program. Consequently, a number of communities are receiving special financial assistance, as a result of having been designated under ILAP.
Recent employment figures have identified the communities of Kamloops, B.C., and Salmon Arm, B.C. with unemployment rates of 27 per cent and 30 per cent respectively. These unemployment levels are the highest in Canada. These communities have therefore been ravaged by unemployment more than most. To seek relief, both formal and informal requests
for designation under ILAP have been made. To date these appeals have fallen on deaf ears.
The questions which spring to mind are: first, how devastated must a community be before it is designated under ILAP and, second, is the designation under ILAP based on a community's need, or is it designated under the auspices of patronage?

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED FORMATION OF PRODUCTIVITY COUNCIL
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, during this harsh economic time it is especially significant to note that Canada stands alone among the major industrialized nations in that it does not have some form of national productivity centre.
As the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated in his three talks to the nation, improvement in the country's economy, especially in regard to our international trading position, requires, in part, an improvement in Canadian productivity. I would like therefore to suggest that the federal Government, in co-operation with the Provinces and other business and labour groups, consider the formation of a Canadian productivity council. Such a council could have as its goals: first, to raise the country's level of productivity consciousness; second, to act as a clearing house for productivity research and literature; and third, to establish centres across the country and offer short courses in productivity improvement.
These goals would in turn encourage both business and labour to increase productivity, decrease the per unit cost of our goods and services, and thereby increase the competitiveness of Canadian goods and services both at home and abroad which would help to spur on the Canadian economy and employment opportunities.

subsubtopic: CAPITAL GAINS TAX ON FARMLAND
speechtext:
Most
Canadians, including many MPs, believe Canada has enormous agricultural land. That belief is totally untrue and is very dangerous. On a global scale, Canada has only 3 per cent of the world's arable land. Canada has less agricultural land than Western Europe, and one-seventh that of the U.S.A. Within Canada only 13 per cent of our land is arable, and only 4 per cent of that is class one or two.
The yearly loss of agricultural land is enormous. It is over 30,000 acres. The number of farmers has dropped 55 per cent since 1941 to some 318,000.
Liberal Party economic policies have resulted in over 50 per cent of our farmers having to earn income off their farms to
January 19, 1983

survive. The most recent attack on farmers is the capital gains tax. In fact it is a tax on capital, because inflation has been the reason for increased land values and not productivity.
It is now almost impossible for a farmer to keep a farm together as one unit and pass it on to the next generation. Capital gains tax is a time bomb which will result in Canadians standing in food lines. The solution, and it is essential to our national well-being, is for the capital gains tax to be abolished on bona fide farmland. This will encourage small family farms which, in turn, will buy machinery from Canadian manufacturers. It will also result in farms being better managed, and in a higher percentage of food self-sufficiency.
Fellow MPs, let us act together now so our descendants will be proud of us and not curse us from bread lines.

Madam Speaker, to begin with, just commenting briefly on the report from the Metro Toronto Social Planning Council, they have not sent me a full copy, but I have seen news reports of it. We have to be very careful with such reports that we do not distort the figures and exaggerate them beyond what the reality is in order to frighten people.
What they do include in that report is what they call the discouraged workers and underemployed workers. That includes a lot of people, who have gone back to school to improve their education and training during that period of time, so I believe we have to be very careful. That does not in any way diminish the seriousness or the critical factor that there are a lot of people out of work, and we must work together to bring them back into jobs.
One of the major achievements we have made over the last several months is in working closely together with the provincial Governments to co-ordinate our efforts, to provide for a combination of resources, to do joint planning so that we can work together to use the maximum amount of governmental resources in this area.
We are now engaged in a meeting with the private sector, with business and labour, to see if we can develop systems to bring that about with them as well. It will only work, Madam Speaker, if we have that kind of partnership and not the kind of rhetoric which the Leader of the Opposition too often uses.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture or to his parliamentary secretary. More than a year ago, the Danish pork-producing industry was struck by an epidemic, and as a result, production was increased in Canada. speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Dionne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subsubtopic: STATE OF DISEASE AFFECTING PIGS IN DENMARK
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in 1982, an epidemic did, indeed, cause a number of problems in Denmark, and this country has just confirmed that the epidemic still exists, since last week, 120 cases were reported among hogs and seventy-two cases among calves, all of which were slaughtered this week. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Senior Canadian National officials earlier this week advised the Government of Prince Edward Island of their plans to transfer most of the Island's heavy freight operations from the Island to Moncton, New Brunswick, as part of an over-all rationalization of services within that region and Quebec. Given that that measure, if it goes ahead, will render Prince Edward Island the only Province in Canada without a fully operational carload
Oral Questions
centre, will the Minister undertake to exercise every possible moral suasion with Canadian National officials in Montreal to have this disastrous decision reversed?

subsubtopic: TRANSFER OF HEAVY FREIGHT OPERATIONS FROM PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND TO NEW BRUNSWICK
speechtext: I must admit, Madam Speaker, that the Hon. Member has a very special way of introducing that question which makes my answer a little more difficult than it otherwise would have been. But each time that three or four or five jobs are lost in the CN there is a question or protest of this kind. My answer is always the same, that if my hon. friend wants CN to be viable and to give Canadian shippers the best possible rates, the lowest possible rates, they have to allow the Corporation to make these technological and administrative changes. In this particular instance it affects ten people, three of whom are going to stay in Charlottetown, two are being relocated, and the other five will be given the usual pre-retirement and retraining opportunities.

Madam Speaker, I will put a supplementary question to the Minister of Transport. It is not just a few jobs that are involved; it is a question of whether we are going to have an essential service for the Island and an important part of the economic base of the Province.
Given that Island shippers require on-the-spot, direct, personal, day-to-day services provided by CN employees on the Island, rather than having those services provided by computers in some other part of Canada, and instead of echoing some rationale given to him by the head office of CN in Montreal, would the Minister take the initiative to investigate the matter himself? At the moment he is just echoing something said to him by people who have a vested interest in taking apart the railway in P.E.I.
Madam Speaker, I take some objection to the tone of the question, but I will not answer in kind. I am too generous and too cool to do that sort of thing.
That is why you ignored the CTC on VIA Rail.

This is not a position that was imposed upon me by CN. I dare say that people in P.E.I. really believe, as I do, that these changes have to be made if potatoes, other agricultural products or the manufactured goods of P.E.I. are to be shipped at the best possible price. I think that this a strong belief throughout Canada. It has the name of productivity, if my hon. friend is looking for an expression to characterize it.
There is no law in the Constitution which indicates that all provinces should have centres of all Crown corporations of the country. There are other cases where centres are not located in every province in Canada. This is one of those instances, and I regret it. I prefer to be charming, but in this instance I think that the importance of the best possible rates for shippers is the predominant pre-occupation.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Communications. Last fall the Minister was very bellicose in making attacks on pubs and other institutions which had unlicensed earth stations. What has happened since then?

Madam Speaker, as the Hon. Member is aware, our policy is aimed at protecting cable distributors who are licensed by the Canadian Government against unfair competition from people who pirate programs and try to retransmit them, thus competing with licensed cable distributors. There are a number of cases which will come before the courts in February, including one in Chicoutimi and another involving the Holiday Inn in Winnipeg. Meanwhile, as the Hon. Member is aware, the Newfoundland Court of Appeal has confirmed that as far as the reception of programs via satellite is concerned, the Canadian Government has full jurisdiction.
It appears that the Minister has huffed and puffed, but he has yet to blow the house down.
Madam Speaker, I want to ask the Minister specifically how many charges have been laid, since last fall, as a result of his threats against the owners of unlicensed earth stations.

Madam Speaker, following the statement I made last autumn, we got in touch with a number of people who were using antennae without getting permission from the CRTC and without a licence from the Department of Communications. I remember at least two hotels in the Toronto area which ceased such operations at our request, and there have been other cases in Canada where an order from the Department or the CRTC has put an end to such illegal activity.
I should hope, Madam Speaker, that it will not always be necessary to take legal action in order to make people comply with the law. I believe that now the Canadian Government has successfully put its case to the courts in Newfoundland and in a number of other instances, people will be more likely to comply with the requirements of our legislation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext:
that Bill C-665, an Act to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
She said: Madam Speaker, the Private Member's Bill which I have before the House this afternoon, Bill C-665, comes, I would say, at a particularly propitious time. I make that statement, of course, because of the very great concern which surrounds the takeover of certain trust companies based in Toronto and the increased attention that has been paid to that matter in recent days. I would also suggest that that concern has been in the public domain for quite a time.
The purpose of my Bill-and this will explain why it comes at such a propitious time-is to amend the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act so as to increase present insurance coverage for depositors from $20,000 to $100,000. This is a move which is long overdue. The insurance coverage under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act has really not been changed since the Act was brought into effect back in 1967, even though the $20,000 coverage that was established some 15 years ago is totally unrealistic given today's economic realities. A sum of $20,000 in 1967 dollars no longer has anything like that value today; it is perhaps 40 per cent of the value of $20,000 in 1967. Therefore, it has no relevancy to the needs of today.
I reiterate, sir, that this increase is long overdue. Arguments favouring such a move have come from a variety of sources over a considerable period of time, and rightly so. They have come because of inflation, high interest rates, rampant unemployment and huge deficits. These things have all contributed to the very uncertain economic climate in which Canadians exist today. These are the conditions which have caused Canadians to view their economic security with anxiety and concern. That concern is not limited solely to the vast national problems that affect this country. It is not limited to the economic instability and uncertainty that one hears being expressed from coast to coast. It centres more and more upon the personal financial security of individuals. People are
wondering how they are going to stand in relation to their own future.
That concern was expressed long before the recent developments with regard to Crown Trust, Greymac Trust and Seaway Trust. Obviously those developments which have taken place in recent days have aggravated the concern considerably. But for much of the last year and indeed before that 1 was being questioned more and more often by people in my own riding and by groups to whom I have spoken elsewhere about the security of their deposits with banks and trust companies.
It was in response to those repeatedly expressed concerns that I introduced this Private Members' Bill, hoping that it might be given serious consideration and, indeed, that it would be given acceptance by the Government. In so doing, it would give assurance as well to the individuals concerned that their life savings, in whatever form they might be, whether as RRSPs or as deposits in banks, would not be in any jeopardy.
Canadians are only too well aware that the country has been on an economic roller coaster for some years now. The time has come, therefore, to strengthen some of the safety features which are supposedly in place to protect Canadians. Obviously, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act is one such measure which needs strengthening. If that measure is going to be there to protect Canadians, then we ought to do what it says we will do, and that is, protect them. At the moment the $20,000 limit does not. What I am suggesting today would help to meet that protection.
Various proposals have been put forward over the years to achieve that goal. My Bill is one such proposal. It would increase the coverage for insurance from $20,000 to $100,000. This proposal does not originate with me; it has been presented by many people and it has been well argued by several organizations. The Consumers' Association of Canada is one such organization that has put forward this proposal.
Tom Delaney, the economic policy adviser for the Consumers Association of Canada, was quoted in an article which appeared in The Globe and Mail on Monday, January 10, 1983. He said that the federal Government should immediately strengthen its deposit insurance protection limits to $100,000 and iron out confusion in the legislation to avert what he calls a crisis of confidence in the trust industry. He is quoted as having said the following:
I'm not saying this is the doomsday scenario, but it's the kind of thing that demonstrates the reason for the CAC's concern over the years.
Concern has been expressed repeatedly by Mr. Delaney and others.
It is my understanding that the Canadian Bankers' Association has suggested increasing the coverage to $40,000 with unlimited coverage for RRSPs. I may be misinterpreting their position, and if so, I am sorry. But if I am correct in my interpretation of what they would like to see instituted, then that is a proposal well worth considering.
This afternoon the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) finally got around to introducing a Government bill
January 19, 1983

to raise the coverage by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation from $20,000 to $60,000 with protection being retroactive to January 17, 1983. He is the latest in a series of individuals to make proposals along this line. Though I am glad to see the Government is finally taking some positive steps toward reviewing the present insurance arrangement, I am concerned about several factors of that Bill.
First, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid), who also has a Private Members' Bill before the House on this subject, said earlier today in the House, there is some question as to whether or not there would be adequate protection for depositors under the retroactive legislation proposed by the Minister.
In a Toronto Star article dated January 18, 1983, Mr. Robert Hammond, a Director of the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation and Superintendent of Insurance, said that until the legislation is passed in the House of Commons depositors will still be limited to $20,000, although they will be protected to $60,000. As a result of this difference in opinion as to the actual protection available, I point to the urgency for this House to end the uncertainty for depositors. That uncertainty can indeed be ended by sending this Bill to committee so that the issue can be studied and adequate protection established at the earliest possible moment. Canadian investors must have that insurance. There exists too much uncertainty today. For instance, how long would it take an investor to be reimbursed for any loss by the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation; and would the reimbursement include interest for the period of time that the investor has to wait for the payment to be made? Those are questions which further aggravate the uncertainty.
Two concerns have been expressed to me about my Bill, Mr. Speaker. One is that it would cause a very significant increase in the premiums that would have to be paid by the chartered banks on insurance deposits which they have in the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. While I sympathize with their dilemma, I am confident of their ability to meet it.
The other concern that has been expressed is that the increase in insurance coverage to $100,000 may, in itself, add to the anxiety and uncertainty of depositors. In other words, it might cause alarm that a crisis may be imminent. My Bill is intended to do just the opposite. The anxiety and the uncertainty exists already. They are there and cannot be denied. The best way to overcome them is to provide the security that investors have a right to expect. I know of no better way to accomplish this than to send this Bill to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs this very afternoon so that we can get on with implementing its provisions and introduce a level of insurance that will guarantee protection to investors so that the uncertainty and anxiety which exists in the country will be erased.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise to speak in this very important debate concerning the security of the deposits which Canadians have
Deposit Insurance
in our financial institutions. This important issue has been considered in previous deliberations in the very committee to which the Hon. Member would like to send her Bill, the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs. We undertook that study during our deliberations on the question of bank profits when all Members of the House were represented in the Committee. At the time of the report, one of the Parties had decided to withdraw. Certainly the Members of the Official Opposition and the Government were represented during those deliberations and they concurred entirely in the recommendations.
It was made clear by both Members of the Official Opposition and the Government during our discussion on the question of deposit insurance that a $60,000 limit was adequate, given the purpose for which deposit insurance is in place and the changes which have occurred since 1967 when deposit insurance was established at $20,000 per institution, with some exceptions. The existing law has been changed as a result of the announcement by the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Cosgrove) on Monday, when he indicated that any deposit in place from Monday onward would be covered by the new limits, which have been raised to $60,000 from $20,000.
The question we were concerned with at the committee deliberations was the limit at which deposit insurance should be set in order to provide adequate coverage. One can see the necessity for deposit insurance when its history is reviewed. Deposit insurance was originally established in the 1930s, primarily at the initiative of the United States but in Canada as well. The difficulties faced in the United States were much more serious since bank failures had taken place in that country. Authorities in the United States were much more fearful that, if no protection were provided for a depositor's funds in financial institutions, there would continue to be runs on institutions whenever there was a rumour that depositors' funds may not be safe in a particular institution which might not have been able to reimburse the full value of a deposit.
In Canada, our track record in this regard has been much better. I believe that the last bank failure occurred in the mid-1920s and it was a relatively small bank.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext: What about trust companies?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext: Our institutions have been solvent and have not experienced any problems of failure-except for the recent example that the Hon. Member just mentioned of Astra Trust.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext: What about Argosy?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext:
Canadian depositors have been very well protected by the institutions. In addition, however, deposit insurance has been in place up to the amount of $20,000. This deposit insurance is structured in such a way that $20,000 is not the total coverage that is available to an individual who has means in excess of $20,000. For example, this means that a depositor can have a deposit at an institution with coverage at all branches of the institution, whether a bank or trust company, up to a maximum of $20,000, but that person's spouse can also have coverage in the same institution for accounts in

January 19, 1983
Deposit Insurance
that person's name of up to $20,000. As well, they can both have a third joint account which is also covered. Under the old rules, this meant that a person and their spouse could be covered up to a maximum at that time of three times $20,000 or $60,000.
In addition to that, the deposit insurance limits apply to the value of deposits in a particular institution. Therefore, if a person deposits up to $20,000 in one institution, they are covered; if they deposit $20,000 in a second institution and $20,000 in a third institution, they are also covered. This means that a person can achieve total coverage equal to the amount of their deposit, whether $100,000 or $200,000, by splitting deposits among different institutions.
The difficulty that arose was that the increase in inflation and salaries gave rise to increased savings and the limit of $20,000 became very inappropriate. For example, the three-year maximum limit of RRSP contributions would amount to approximately $15,000 or $16,000 plus interest, and a person could exceed the total value of the deposit insurance in that institution very quickly. This is a result of the limits remaining unchanged since 1967 while inflation has certainly escalated the amount of savings and income available.
During the review of this whole question in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs' study of bank profits, the Members of the Committee unanimously agreed, as appears at page 21 of the Committee hearings, that:
Deposit insurance is also important as a means of protecting depositors' savings.
Here, we were referring to the whole question of bank solvency and bank liquidity, but we were not just concerned with chartered banks. We had broadened our scope implicitly to include the solvency and financial integrity of all financial institutions which accepted deposits. The Committee went on to say:
Since it was first implemented in 1967, the value of the protection this insurance offers to depositors has been seriously eroded by inflation. The Committee therefore recommends that:
8. Deposit insurance should be increased to afford a better real protection of depositors' savings. The level of insurance for each individual depositor with any bank should be raised from the present $20,000 to at least $60,000, which restores the real value of protection offered when it was introduced in 1967. The level of deposit insurance should be reviewed every five years.
I believe that was a very good recommendation. It was responsible in light of all of the facts. It certainly goes to restore the real value of the protection that was provided.
I would note that this recommendation is fully reflected in the Bill that the Hon. Minister introduced in the House today and in the statement that he made on Monday with regard to the Bill that the limits have now been increased to $60,000 as recommended. While I have not yet seen the Bill, I urge that there should be some protection for an automatic review of those ceiling limits if that is not in the Bill. There should be some provision for automatic review of those ceiling limits every five years, as we have recommended in the committee report. Every five years we should review the limits of deposit insurance coverage and then we would not get ourselves back into the position we are now facing. Such was the motivation
behind the Bill presented by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald). Fifteen or sixteen years after the fact we are just getting around to modifying those limits.
We in the committee felt very strongly that not only should the limits be increased, but there should also be an automatic provision in the Bill that the question concerning limits and their adequacy should be brought before Parliament at least once every five years.
Therefore, the question is whether the Government Bill and the raising of the limit from $20,000 to $60,000 is adequate or whether those limits should be further raised to $100,000. I do not think it is necessary to raise those limits to $100,000. I have noted Mr. Delaney's comments, a man I have known for a long time. I respect his work for the Consumers' Association and as a private consultant in the field of financial affairs.
The other night, on "The Journal", I believe Mr. Delaney indicated that the Government's action was too little, too late. I do not agree that it is either too little or too late because certainly, now that we have increased the limit to $60,000 through the multiple family accounts which I described earlier, a person, with his or her spouse, could obtain coverage in a single institution up to $180,000. On the other hand, by simply splitting the accounts across three institutions, for example, a bank, a trust company, and another trust company or bank, which can now be done efficiently because the amounts which we are discussing are large enough, the individual can again be covered up to $180,000, or, across four institutions, up to $240,000.
These limits, these amounts, go far beyond the financial savings of the vast majority of Canadians, and I also think it is good, sound financial practice, for purposes of financial planning and management, for people not to place all of their savings in one institution. It is a good idea to diversify those savings across several institutions and several kinds of investment vehicles, such as five-year guaranteed investment certificates, perhaps self-administered registered retirement savings plans of various forms, or short-term savings certificates. Various forms of financial instruments should be invested in when one is considering the volumes of money we are discussing here under the new coverage. Certainly, a person would be wise to spread those moneys across institutions simply because different institutions have different performance patterns. In order to get a good average rate of return representing what can be achieved from the marketplace, so to speak, it is a good idea to diversify.
Certainly, the coverage we are now asking Parliament to approve in the Minister's Bill today, $60,000, would provide adequate coverage for a very sound investment in any one institution and would allow efficient splitting of savings across institutions, whereas the $20,000 limit clearly did not and needed to be raised. It caused people to find it necessary to distribute their savings of, say, $100,000 or $110,000 in RRSP
January 19, 1983

across five, six or seven institutions. Not only is that inefficient, but it is also difficult for the individual to administer that kind of fund. It also adds to the cost of the institutions involved and thereby lowers the return which could be paid to savers. This is because if an institution has many small accounts of $15,000, for example, instead of a few larger accounts, its cost of doing business increases. It either lowers the rate which can be paid on savings, or it tends to increase the rate paid on loans. Not only do we want to try to make the system fair, equitable and safe for Canadian savers, but we also want to try to make the system efficient from the point of view of the Canadian financial institutions so that the rates of interest charged on loans are the lowest they could possibly be and the rates on savings are the highest they could possibly be.
I think the amendment by the Minister to the Act is an adequate one. It is one which was very strongly recommended by the Finance Committee, there being unanimous agreement of its members. I might add that there was no logical argument against this proposal given to us by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands other than the fact that the United States has a limit of $100,000. I think there are some other differences of which she may be aware between how deposit insurance is handled in the United States and how it is handled here. It is also a fact that Mr. Delaney of the Consumer's Association of Canada has recommended a limit of $100,000.1 believe the basis of his recommendation is that that is the limit in the United States.
I believe that with the amendment concerning the limit proposed by the Minister of $60,000, in fact the one which is now in place for Canadian depositors, we will be able to provide adequate protection for deposits of any size if they are split in the way I have suggested. I do not see any need to impose additional cost on financial institutions by raising the limit from $60,000 to $100,000, so I do not see the logic in the argument in favour of $100,000. Certainly, in 1967 there was logic in setting the rate at $20,000. The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands said that that has now been depreciated to 40 per cent of its original value in real terms, which would mean that it has been dropped down to real coverage of $8,000. If we multiply that by 2.5, it is once again $20,000, which would be full coverage. Therefore, 2.5 times the 1967 value, according to her figures, would bring it to full value.

speechtext: I am thinking ahead.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext:
However, 2.5 times $20,000 is $50,000, the Minister has proposed a limit of $60,000, and she is proposing $100,000. I suggest that perhaps the Hon. Member's figures are slightly off because we considered that situation, and increasing the limit from $20,000 to $60,000 is very close to being the full readjustment for inflation. I think it is more than 50 per cent. I think the depreciation has come down further than 40 per cent. Therefore, the actual restoration of original value requires that we increase from $20,000 to $60,000 today, and then there would be an automatic review every five years to upgrade or adjust if inflation continues at a high rate, which I certainly do not expect and I know the Government does not. The financial markets certainly are not predicting inflation at
Deposit Insurance
historical rates, so we would expect that there might be some deterioration relative to the same extent as we have experienced lately.
Concerning raising the limits further, beyond $60,000, one must consider that in the way our deposit insurance is structured, all institutions are required to pay about one-thirtieth of 1 per cent on deposit liabilities as a contribution to the fund. That percentage varies depending on the type and size of fund and the necessity of further contributions.
There is another issue involving raising the limit which would affect all institutions, especially those which are marginal and might be in a position to get themselves into trouble, such as the ones in the marketplace which have been the subject of much public and media coverage in the last few months. The argument against raising the limit is that institutions which might have marginal lending and investment practices would then be able to borrow from the public through the form of deposits up to a maximum of $100,000 and would have this public insurance umbrella. The fact is that, as a result of that ability, other institutions would have to pay higher premiums for deposit insurance to provide the coverage necessary to protect the public interest with regard to deposits in some of these more marginal institutions. That kind of redistribution I do not think is right; I do not think it is fair.
We have to provide a balance between causing the stable, sound institutions to subsidize the less stable institutions, and at the same time protect the public interest. I think a $60,000 limit does precisely that. It provides for a sound coverage of deposit insurance and at the same time it does not increase the limits to the extent which would allow some of the more marginal institutions-there are certainly some in Canada and there could be more in the future-to exceed their depth at the expense of a publicly insured deposit situation.
Looking at the actual Canadian experience with deposit insurance, there are some figures as to how much additional benefit the Canadian depositor would receive from going from $60,000 to $100,000. Here are some estimates of the percentage of deposits that would be covered at the various levels of deposit insurance. In the case of banks, with the limit at $60,000, 79 per cent of all deposits in the chartered banks are less than $60,000. When you go to $100,000, you only move from 79 per cent to 83 per cent. So you do not achieve a great deal of increase of protection for Canadians by increasing the limit from $60,000 to $100,000.
In the case of trust companies, 92 per cent of all deposits are less than $60,000 and 95 per cent are less than $100,000. For an additional $40,000 of protection and the costs associated with that, you only increase the percentage of total deposits covered by 3 per cent, whether it be with banks or with trust companies.
I think that the possibility of splitting deposits efficiently now, with the new limits of $60,000, and the fact that the vast majority of deposits are being covered by these limits, means that we should support the Government Bill to increase these

January 19, 1983
Deposit Insurance
limits to $60,000. I suggest that if we could get together in the Steering Committee on Finance and come to an agreement, I can see no reason why we could not give the Government Bill all three readings in very short order.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be brief in order that we can move this Bill quickly into the Finance Committee for rapid passage, but I do want to make two or three comments. The Bill is long overdue but I am encouraged that this Bill, which was brought forward by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), is finally before us.
The Committee to which the previous speaker referred tabled the study into bank profits earlier in the summer, and only on Monday did the Government see fit to bring in their Bill. I wonder if the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands had not introduced this Bill whether that kind of action would have been seen. But whatever the reason, we are now dealing with this very important matter in an effort to bring some stability and to build confidence in Canada. To say that there is a feeling of uncertainty in the country would be an oversimplification. Indeed, for many people in this country there is a certain sense of fear. The takeover of the assets of the three trust companies by the Province of Ontario recently does little to dispel that fear and the most haste we can bring to bear on this Bill will be in the best interests of developing security and hope for the future of Canada.
I have very little interest in the debate on whether or not the maximum should be $60,000 or $100,000. I think that is a point open for some discussion. I have listened to the two previous speakers who have made a strong case for one or the other. I suppose I feel at the moment that $60,000 would be an appropriate figure, for a number of reasons. I understand that a $60,000 maximum would in fact cover about 92 per cent of deposits in trust companies. Raising the limit to $100,000 would move that figure up to 95 per cent, and for that 3 per cent difference, and considering the extra premiums that would be expected from the institutions, I am not certain that is really necessary at this point.
I, along with others, have received a great number of representations, both from trust companies and from individuals who are very concerned. My colleagues from Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen) and the Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Anguish) have expressed the concerns of their constituents. A typical example could involve a man and wife who have on deposit with one of the controversial trust companies, Greymac, about $55,000. Under the present legislation they are not fully protected. They are viewing this as retirement income and are bringing to their Member's attention their concern and urging him to press for raising that deposit
insurance from $20,000 to $60,000, or higher. Again I say that at $40,000 or $60,000 I believe a case can be made for either one.
I listened with interest to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands who I believe referred to the $100,000 coming from the American model. While we recognize that the United States banking and financial system generally is quite different from ours in Canada, being more along monopoly lines I suppose one of the benefits is that it does provide more security as opposed to the small, independent banks in the United States.
With the $60,000 limit a couple could have security for $180,000 in terms of each individual having an independent deposit protection of $60,000, as well as sharing a joint deposit with the $60,000 coverage.
As other speakers have suggested, spreading one's deposits among various institutions simply reflects good business practice and is probably in their best interest. Again, a $60,000 maximum would probably provide one with all the coverage one may need to expect.
I do appreciate the initiative which has been taken by the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands. I would like to see this Bill referred to committee today and let us get on with it quickly and get it back into the House. I know that as a steering committee we will have no difficulty in negotiating a $60,000 or $100,000 sum. Then we can get the Bill back into the House for rapid passage, preferably without debate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend from Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) will note that the Speaker called me the Member for Mississauga! It depends how the representation is in the city.
There are two questions which have been raised in this debate which I think should be dealt with immediately. First is the question whether the limit should be $60,000 or $100,000. Our friend from Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) suggested that the difference was not that much in terms of the numbers of people being covered. He said that 92 per cent of the trust company deposits were less than $60,000 and that 95 per cent of them were less than $100,000. So the Hon. Member asked, why not make it just $60,000? The answer, of course, is why not make it $100,000, because the additional risk is quite minimal. So why not go for the $100,000?
The second question he raised concerned the decision to make the limit $60,000. I remind him that that was before it became eminently apparent that the Government had lost track of its management responsibilities in the money markets. There is a real fear, concern and lack of confidence that has developed, and it is essential that we do something and do it well in order to restore that confidence. I say that $60,000 does not have the ring of confidence that $100,000 has. As the
January 19, 1983

Member for Ottawa Centre pointed out, the cost is not that much different.
The Government has a responsibility to supervise these companies. One way of ensuring that supervision is carried out is to increase the liability of the Government for its failure to supervise. That can easily be done by changing the terms of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act to $100,000. That $100,000 will give real assurance that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will look at the securities held by trust and loan companies and make sure that they are properly policed. They have not been properly policed.
We have seen that with the incorporation of Greymac and Seaway by this Government. Seaway was incorporated in 1982. It was not incorporated in 1981. Imagine a company being incorporated in 1982 and before even a year had elapsed it has already had seized its assets and responsibility for deposits. That is a clear indication of lack of attention to detail by that ministry. It is important to restore confidence. This Bill is an attempt to do that.
The next question is, why not proceed instead with the Government legislation? I remind Hon. Members that the Government has been attempting to end this session of Parliament since November, so it says. There are some 18 or 19 Bills which the House Leader has indicated are essential, even though this session is to end relatively early in February. Where will we get time to deal with that piece of legislation? The probability is that, having introduced the legislation and having made a fuss about introducing it, the Government will do as it did with the Bankruptcy Act and a whole series of other statutes. They leave them on the Order Paper. They boasted about them, sent out pamphlets, did their PR work, but they have not been passed.
If this House really intends to deal with deposit insurance and intends to get down to the business of increasing the limit, why not take advantage of this Bill, pass it at second reading and get it to committee? Amendments can easily be made in committee, hearings held quickly, the Bill brought back to the House and the matter dealt with.
The Government has a shortage of House time. We are suggesting that this is an opportunity to take advantage of Private Members' time to get what amounts to Government legislation through the House now. To make sure the Private Members' hour does not elapse, I will resume my seat and let this Bill come to a vote.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few comments on this Bill. May I say at the beginning that I welcome it, and I welcome some of the comments that have been made. A few moments before the debate began we heard the Speaker say she had some reservations about this Bill and would have to pass judgment on it if it got as far as a vote. I take those directions from Madam Speaker very seriously. However, we can be assured that the debate today
Deposit Insurance
has been most useful and welcome in light of the tabling of the Government's Bill earlier today in the House. This has been a constructive joining of efforts to advance the issue and clear up some of the comments on it.
I extend my congratulations to the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) for her obvious concern about this topic and to the other speakers who rose to comment. We all join in trying to clear the air at a time of uncertainty and to give the ordinary depositor and the ordinary Canadian a sense that the safety net of deposit insurance is intact and satisfactory.
Along that vein, I would like to refer to an editorial in the Toronto Star of January 18, yesterday, entitled "And Ottawa's reassuring step". I quote:
Given the concerns raised by Consumer and Commercial Relations Minister Robert Elgie's statement yesterday, Ottawa's decision to triple the level of protection for people who entrust their money to financial institutions comes not a moment too soon.
I quote from the end of the same editorial:
It is vital that people be able to have full faith in our financial institutions and not have to fear the slightest possibility that their life's savings could be wiped out at a strike, through no fault of their own. Cosgrove's announcement is a reassuring step in that direction.
There are two initial comments that can be made about this present debate. First, as I have already said, we welcome the opportunity to debate this question. Second, we are grateful to the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) and other Members of the Finance Committee for the hard work they did on the bank profits study which provided much of the factual background for a Bill such as the one before us.
The increase to $60,000 does give much of the reassurance that the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) is seeking for ordinary savers. It is important and notable that 92 per cent of all the deposits in trust companies are covered by the $60,000 limit. Equally important, almost 79 per cent of bank deposits are covered by that limit.
As the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) pointed out, that is an important emphasis for the trust companies, which appear to be much more vulnerable than the banks. As he said, it is an important benefit that we get from the Canadian banking system. When a community suffers an economic setback, the banking system in that community does not become vulnerable. People's savings are protected by these large banks and the strength of the whole system is applied to the individual community.
There is a different system in the United States. They have community-located banks which are more vulnerable than our banks. They are not able to bring this national strength to bear when a local community runs into economic difficulty.
The fact that 92 per cent of the trust and loan company deposits are covered by this $60,000 dealing is significant. It is no secret that for some time the Government has been considering the question of increasing this ceiling. The Government's Bill, the one introduced today, applies additional insurance protection to the existing deposits in those Ontario trust

January 19, 1983
Deposit Insurance
companies which are currently in difficulty and, as a result, their depositors are not going to suffer.
Now, before I go further, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out some important aspects of the deposit insurance provided by the CDIC. The Corporation was established by federal legislation in 1967, in the wake of the failure of another Ontario trust company in which a considerable number of people lost their savings. Membership in the Corporation is restricted to banks, trust companies and mortgage loan companies. It is mandatory for federally-incorporated companies. Provincially-incorporated trust and mortgage loan companies must apply for membership and they are accepted only if the Government of their Province has approved the application and certain standards and conditions are met.
Deposits with companies in Quebec which are incorporated by that Province are covered by the deposit insurance plan administered by the Quebec Deposit Insurance Board. Obviously, the main difference between the Bill we are debating today and the Government's new proposal involves the amount of the maximum limit of deposits covered by insurance.
The Hon. Member today in her Bill proposes that the present $20,000 limit be escalated up to $100,000. The Government in the Bill we introduced today suggests that the ceiling be increased to $60,000. This is the amount which was recommended, as we have discussed, by the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs in the report on July 27 on bank profits. It is a reasonable amount, reflecting the increases in incomes, prices and savings since the deposit insurance plan was begun in 1967.
Interestingly enough, The Toronto Star in that same editorial estimates that the $20,000 limit would translate from 1967 to today at approximately $63,000. There are additional factors, however, which argue in favour of the $60,000 maximum. One of the most important considerations relates to the basic purpose of the deposit insurance scheme. The goal of the 1967 legislation, and the goal we should be seeking today, is to provide substantial insurance for the savings of average Canadians.
The plan recognizes that ordinary Canadians should be able to deposit their savings in our basic financial institutions with the confidence that their money will be safe. Ordinary Canadians should not have to equip themselves with sophisticated skills and knowledge so as to reassure themselves that this kind of savings deposit can be made with assurance.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext: On a point of order, would the Hon. Member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) accept a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE BASIC DEPOSIT COVERAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to accept a question from my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South, my compatriot from that beautiful city, but perhaps he would be courteous enough to let me finish my remarks and then I would love to hear from him. It would be a great pleasure.
I suggest that people with individual investments as large as $100,000 can reasonably be expected either to have some knowledge of financial markets, or go to someone who does have that knowledge and equip themselves with that knowledge.
The extent of coverage being provided, even with the existing $20,000 ceiling, really is substantial. We heard from the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) along those lines. With the $20,000 limit, CDIC estimates that there is a total insurance protection for 63 per cent of bank deposits and 76 per cent of trust and loan company deposits. The proposed $60,000 ceiling would mean that approximately 79 per cent of bank deposits would be insured, and trust and loan companies would include 92 per cent of the deposits.
I would point out that even the average investor is not so unsophisticated that he or she is unaware that there are very simple ways of ensuring insurance protection for amounts of savings greater than the $20,000 limit, or $60,000 under the new proposal. Since the limit applies to the total of deposits which an individual has in his or her name within a single institution, that person can simply place extra amounts on deposit in another institution. Even within a single institution, a married person is insured to the maximum amount in his or her own name, and at the same time has the maximum insurance in a joint account held by both spouses. To carry the point further, the other spouse may have a third account insured to the maximum. Therefore, by using three different accounts, a married couple, under the $60,000 ceiling, is insured for up to a total of $180,000 in a single institution. Given these facts, it can hardly be argued that the $60,000 limit is unreasonably low and will not provide the means for adequate insurance protection for the savings of a vast majority of Canadians.
The argument is also made, and was made here today, that because of the large amounts of savings accumulated in recent years in Registered Retirement Savings Plans, and to a lesser extent in Home Ownership Savings Plans, the insurance maximum should be tailored to better accommodate RRSPs. That would not be a wise course for a number of reasons. We should bear in mind that deposits in RRSPs and RHOSPs can be invested in a variety of ways, not only via an insured account in CDIC member institutions. Assets of RRSPs which are invested in this way are insured separately from any other deposit of the holder of the RRSP; thus such an individual has up to $60,000 of insurance for the RRSP savings in such a plan, on top of the other insurance for ordinary deposits outside the RRSP. To provide a higher ceiling for RRSP savings would obviously bias and distort the decisions which are now made as to how RRSP funds are invested. Furthermore, it would discriminate against the very large number of employer/employee pension plans which cover a large proportion of our working force and which do not have similar insurance guarantees for their solvency.
One other essential question must also be addressed in judging a proper limit for this kind of insurance protection.
January 19, 1983

That point involves the need in our system of financial institutions to encourage good management and sound financial practices. That point can hardly be over-estimated in light of recent occurrences in Ontario. It is unreasonable to expect that the federal and provincial agencies which supervise trust and loan companies can on their own ensure the soundness of all the investment decisions made by every company. That would require an army of inspectors. Therefore, we must ensure that the broad rules under which these companies operate are such as to encourage prudent investment decisions within the industry. In other words, we should not be concerned that the limits for deposit insurance are not so high that they serve to encourage speculative investments or firms with inadequate financial resources and weak management. There must be fairness and balance in the system.
Bear in mind that the CDIC insurance fund is financed through premiums from its member institutions. The large, strong institutions which hold the great majority of deposits are, therefore, the principal source of funds for the CDIC. Even without the insurance system, their deposits could be considered secure. It would, therefore, be difficult to justify forcing such institutions to contribute to a fund that would underwrite the operations of smaller and weaker institutions, if we are talking about insuring a deposit of $100,000.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED DEDUCTION FOR VOLUNTARY FIREMEN
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of amending the Income Tax Act in order to allow voluntary firemen to deduct from their income $1,000 for all expenses incurred in the exercise of their duties.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure to address the above motion which I originally made on April 15, 1980 under the then Standing Order 15.
1 have a soft spot in my heart for firefighters in this country, Mr. Speaker, particularly volunteer firefighters. I wish to recognize the service they provide and, if I may, I will relate a story to the House.
Last March, at eight o'clock one morning as I was getting ready to come up to the Hill, the fire alarm went off in the apartment building in which I live in Ottawa. Anyone who
Volunteer Firemen
lives in an apartment building knows that the fire alarm goes off quite often. This time, however, I opened the door to check and found the hall filled with smoke and the apartment next to mine on fire. I ran down the hall, grabbed the hose and at full speed headed for the apartment, only to find that the hose was about 40 feet too short to reach it and so I fell flat on my fanny. By this time the fire was well under way and the smoke filled the hallways.
If anyone has ever been in a fire they will know just what I am talking about. It is not a situation I should like to experience again. However, it gave me a far greater appreciation of the dangers that firefighters have to face. It also showed me, in very dramatic detail, what damage smoke can do to an apartment and to clothes. There was a total of $4,000 smoke damage done to my apartment alone. I can now appreciate the damage done to the personal belongings of people who go to fight fires. This reinforces my feelings about the importance of firefighters, particularly volunteer firefighters, and what they go through.
In 1975, at the sixtieth annual conference of The Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs, a resolution was introduced by the voluntary sector of the Fire Chiefs' Association of British Columbia regarding an increase in the income tax exemption for all volunteer firemen. 1 will not read the entire motion but at that time a $300 exemption was allowed to volunteer firefighters for expenses incurred as a consequence of their duties. This exemption was introduced about 36 years ago and had not been changed since then. In 1979, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) proposed an increase in the exemption in his now infamous Budget. The proposal, of course, was defeated with the rest of the Budget but it was adopted by the Liberal Government in 1980 when the exemption was increased to $500.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has told us that a Budget will be forthcoming in the not too distant future. I see his Parliamentary Secretary in the House and I am sure he will relay my message to the Minister. The Minister has spoken of having conferences with various interested groups in the country with a view to determining what should be included in the Budget. I hope he will seriously consider including the recommendation made in my motion. An adjustment in the tax exemption for volunteer firefighters is a small way in which these people could be repaid for their dedication and community spirit. I do not think anyone in the House or in the country would deny their importance.
I will dwell on conditions in Ontario because I am most knowledgeable about that Province. In Ontario, fire protection is a municipal responsibility. In fact, under the provisions of the Municipal Act, councils of local municipalities are authorized to establish and regulate fire departments, incur expenditures for capital and operating costs for such services to be paid from local taxes, and decide on the quality and quantity of fire prevention and firefighting services provided to their citizens. For instance, under this system the available statistics, which are for the year 1978-we do not have statistics for

January 19, 1983
Volunteer Firemen
1981-indicate that 8,301,704 people in Ontario were provided with various levels of fire prevention and firefighting services. It should be noted that there is no legal obligation for municipalities to establish a fire department, although in recent years the Canadian Association of Fire Fighters has recommended that firefighting services be made mandatory for municipalities, through legislation.
Most municipalities recognize that they have a social obligation to organize fire protection services. In cases where municipalities have no fire departments of their own, special equipment and firefighting services are purchased through operating agreements with neighbourhood communities.
The basis of what is known as mutual fire aid is pre-planning to provide adequate manpower-in other words, volunteer firefighters and equipment-for given situations and locations, and to use men and equipment as efficiently as possible to the best possible advantage. The pooling of resources underlies the whole system of mutual aid. Mutual fire aid agreements are particularly effective in towns and villages where firefighting facilities are inadequate to handle emergency situations.
I have spoken about the situation in Ontario and I should now like to touch upon the situation in my riding of Brampton-Georgetown, where there are firefighters of whom we can all be proud. Chief Jim Brunne in Brampton and Chief Cunningham in Georgetown are to be congratulated for their dedication and service. Although Brampton is a city of approximately 160,000 citizens, it has 45 volunteer firemen in four different locations. The town of Halton Hills is divided into two areas. In Georgetown there are 45 volunteers and in Acton there are 3'5. These people are so well recognized in Georgetown that the entire volunteer fire brigade was named citizen of the year a few years ago. They are very dedicated people with a great sense of community. These are the ordinary guys who feel that their assistance to the fire department helps everyone.
In Brampton a volunteer is compensated on the points system. He or she earns five points per fire call and five points for attending a training session or for being on weekend duty. The average compensation is from SI50 to $175 per quarter year. They are given $40 per year, which is expected to cover such things as the cleaning of and the wear and tear on clothing. With $40 per year, one smokey fire and the cleaning bill is shot. I saw the bill to clean the clothes that were in my apartment during a fire which caused only smoke damage.
In Georgetown volunteers are given $1,500 per year to cover the wear and tear on clothing and the cost of gasoline. It is interesting to note the difference in what is being paid in compensation in these two communities which are next to one another. To some the compensation may appear to be enough but I do not think to too many. We must be realistic. In Brampton there is an average of three to ten calls per month on volunteer time. In Georgetown there is an average of 200 calls per year. It is a busy fire department. The compensation and tax deduction simply do not cover the actual wear and tear on clothing, the wear and tear on volunteer's cars, the cost of
gasoline and the disruption in volunteers' time. I strongly believe that an increased tax exemption is warranted and would more adequately recognize the services and actual expenses of volunteers.
Volunteer firefighters are not easy to recruit. Every advantage we can give must be given to persons interested in becoming volunteers and to those who are already fighting a very serious threat to us all-fires. The employment of volunteer firefighters, or a combination of full-time and volunteer firefighters in lieu of only full-time firefighters attached to a fire department, can save governments millions of dollars annually. Volunteers are paid only when they are called to the scene of a fire. The saving to Governments which volunteers represent must be acknowledged. The federal Government must do what it can to encourage the continuation of volun-teerism with respect to firefighters. They render a valuable service to the Canadian community at great risk to their own lives. I do not think anyone would argue that. I cannot imagine what many communities would do without volunteers.
The Hon. Member for South West Nova (Miss Campbell) is vitally interested in this particular issue. I gather, because she is present and I know of her interest and involvement in a similar motion, she will speak on it today. Many Members of my caucus have spoken to me over the last number of days because they knew my motion was coming forward. They are vitally interested in the subject. One said, for example, that in his ridings there were 42 volunteer fire departments and only one permanent one. Of course, he and others support this motion and ask that the Government give serious consideration to it and include it in the next Budget.
Just to give an idea of the numbers about which we are talking, the last available figures for Ontario indicated that there were 16,000 part-time volunteer firefighters, and that of 637 municipal fire departments, there were 503 part-time departments employing only volunteer firefighters. These following statistics for other provinces are for 1981. For some reason the other provinces are more up to date than Ontario in their statistics. At the end of 1981, Newfoundland had 4,175 volunteers; Prince Edward Island, 751; Nova Scotia, 7,000; New Brunswick, 3,063; Quebec, 14,771; Manitoba, 2,400; Saskatchewan, 6,000; Alberta, 4,500; British Columbia, 6,500; the Northwest Territories, 750; and Yukon, 150.
We cannot afford to lose these volunteers and the service they provide. It is about time that the Income Tax Act adequately recognized their valuable service to all Canadians. An increased exemption should be considered and included in the forthcoming Budget. The Minister of Finance has an ideal opportunity to win the repect of approximately 67,000 people across Canada through a very simple amendment to the Income Tax Act. I urge him to introduce such an amendment.
As I mentioned earlier, there has only been one change to the tax exemption since its original inception in 1953. That change was proposed in the Budget of the Hon. Member for St. John's West and later adopted by the Liberals. Once again
January 19, 1983

it is time to look at the tax exemption and to increase it to

I should like to point out what this would cost the treasury. It will cost approximately $11 million in lost tax revenue. Just to put that in its perspective, for most of us $11 million is a lot of money but the Government spends $9 million in the time that it takes to hold Question Period-$9 million in 45 minutes. We are asking for a tax exemption which will cost about $11 million or approximately 55 minutes of expenditure by the present Government. We are not asking for something monumental in terms of this tax deduction.
I think we should sum up the services performed by these volunteers. They risk their lives. They interrupt their day-today routines. In some cases they lose pay at their regular jobs each time they answer a fire call. I think it is worthwhile; I doubt that there is a person in Canada who would disagree with that. If the Minister of Finance conducts a survey of every fire marshal or commissioner in Canada, I am certain he would find unanimous approval of such a tax exemption increase.
In summary, I ask for support of this motion by all sides of the House to increase the tax exemption for volunteer firemen to $1,000 in the next federal Budget, which we expect early in the spring.
